## Poker comics

The series index is `/poker/comics/`; the first comic is
`/poker/comics/learn-no-limit-holdem/`. Artwork is hosted locally, unchanged from
the shared Gemini image, at `assets/poker/comics/learn-no-limit-holdem.jpg`
(687 × 1024 pixels). The smaller uploaded PNG was a preview of the same artwork.

For the next approved comic, add its original image to `assets/poker/comics/`,
a source page under `_source/poker/comics/`, and a manifest entry in
`_source/pages.json` with `section: poker`, `poker_comic: true`, an explicit
publication date, and its permanent route. Add its card to
`_source/poker/comics.html`; keep earlier comic URLs and publication dates.
Include a readable text version, attribution and any needed rules clarifications.
Do not describe an AI-generated scene as a recorded hand or personal experience.

The date puts the comic into the existing Poker feed and combined writing feed.
Search indexes derive from the manifest, and Poker search also indexes the text
version. Comic pages use the existing sharing controls. Source and generated HTML
must be rebuilt and committed together using the normal local release checks.

Comic 01 · Published October 14, 2026 A six-panel welcome to the poker table: the deck, the dealer button, the blinds, your hole cards, and your first decision. Read left to right, then down. The artwork simplifies a few rules; the notes and text version below add the details. Learn no-limit Hold’em. Artwork generated with Google Gemini. Open the full image or save the comic . Original Gemini share .

Wait for your turn. The comic’s “all-in at any time” is shorthand. You act only on your turn, and an all-in raise is subject to whether the betting has reopened. No-limit does not remove the betting rules. Blind amounts vary. The big blind is commonly twice the small blind, but use the actual posted structure. With only two players seated, the button posts the small blind and acts first preflop. The drawings are illustrative. Read the captions and explanation for the sequence. Community cards arrive after preflop betting, even though the final panel already shows cards on the table.

This accessible text version follows the six panels and includes the rules clarifications above. Welcome to the table A dealer introduces no-limit Texas Hold’em. This first comic covers setting up a hand and reaching the opening betting round. A standard deck, no jokers The game uses 52 cards. At showdown, compare the best five-card hands made from each player’s two hole cards and the five shared community cards. You may use both, one, or neither of your hole cards. You can also win earlier if every opponent folds. The dealer button and blinds The button marks the dealer position and normally moves clockwise between hands. With three or more players, the next two positions clockwise post the small blind and big blind before the deal. These forced bets start the pot. Live games can use a dead-button procedure when seats become empty. Post the stated amounts The small blind and big blind follow the game’s announced structure. A common example is 100/200: the small blind posts 100 chips and the big blind posts 200. Some games also have an ante, which is separate from the blinds. Two private hole cards Each player receives two cards face down. Keep them private while the hand is in progress. This stage, before the community cards, is called preflop. The first betting round With three or more players, preflop action begins with the first player clockwise after the big blind. On your turn, you may fold, call the amount you face using your available chips, or make a legal raise. If everyone only calls, the big blind may check or raise. Going all-in means committing your remaining chips, subject to the action and betting rules.

The flop brings three community cards, followed by the turn and river, with betting rounds in between when players can still bet. Follow a complete counted hand to see the sequence. For raises and all-ins, use the betting and pots guide . Published by Nolan Kido. Artwork generated with Google Gemini; explanatory text prepared with AI assistance. The scene is fictional and does not depict a recorded hand. This is an introduction, not a complete rulebook. See rules and fair play for rule sources.

Comic 02 · Published October 14, 2026 From royal flush to high card: a comic-style tour of what beats what in standard Texas Hold’em. Poker hand rankings. Artwork generated with Google Gemini. Open the full image or save the comic . Original Gemini share .

The hand categories are in the correct order, but some AI-drawn card faces have inconsistent ranks or suits. Use the written definitions below as your reference. A royal flush is the highest straight flush. Aces can be high or low in a straight: A-K-Q-J-10 or 5-4-3-2-A. They cannot wrap around in Q-K-A-2-3. At a Hold’em showdown, use your best five cards from the seven available. You can use both, one or neither of your hole cards. Suits never break a tie; equal five-card hands share the pot.

This text companion explains each category. The list follows standard high-hand poker, as used in full-deck Texas Hold’em. Royal flush A-K-Q-J-10, all in one suit. Straight flush Five consecutive ranks in one suit. Four of a kind Four matching ranks and a fifth card. Full house Three matching ranks plus a pair. Flush Five cards of one suit, without consecutive ranks. Straight Five consecutive ranks, not all one suit. Three of a kind Three matching ranks and two different side cards. Two pair Two distinct pairs and a fifth card. One pair One pair and three different side cards. High card No pair, straight or flush. Compare highest cards first.

A flush beats a straight. Within a category, compare its key ranks before side cards: for example, compare a full house’s three-of-a-kind rank before its pair. Kickers count only within the best five cards. The poster’s “A Simple Pair can still win!” is a useful reminder: you do not need a spectacular hand to win a pot. You can also win before showdown when every opponent folds. Ranking reference: PokerStars’ standard hand rankings . For practice, try a complete hand from deal to showdown . Published by Nolan Kido. Comic 03 · Published October 14, 2026 Follow a Hold’em hand through preflop, flop, turn and river, then see how showdown or a fold can decide the pot. Poker: One Hand, Four Streets! Artwork generated with Google Gemini. Open the full image or save the comic . Original Gemini share .

The four streets are betting rounds. Showdown is the comparison of hands, not a fifth betting round. A round can check through without anyone making a new bet. If players are all-in and no further betting is possible, the remaining board cards are dealt without more betting. The AI-drawn card faces are not a verified deal. In the showdown panel, K-Q can make a pair of kings with a king on the board, but that alone does not establish a winner. Compare every remaining player’s best five-card hand; equal best hands share the pot. When everyone else folds, the remaining player wins without a showdown and normally does not need to show their cards. Follow the room’s rules about exposing cards.

This accessible companion follows the six panels and explains the sequence. Use the written notes above when the artwork simplifies a rule. Preflop: your two hole cards A new player asks whether another card is coming. The dealer explains that everyone receives two face-down hole cards, then the first betting round takes place. The community-card board is still empty. The flop: three community cards Three face-up cards arrive together. The player wants to see another immediately, but the dealer reminds them that the table must finish this betting round before moving on. The turn: one more card The fourth community card joins the board. The player notices that only one card arrived this time. Another betting round follows. The river: the final card The fifth community card completes the board. The dealer announces the final betting round. Showdown: compare the hands The player says K-Q makes a pair of kings with the king on the board. Another character calls it a winner. That is the comic’s intended ending, but the drawing does not establish the result: a pair wins only if no eligible opponent has a better hand. A hand can end early Two players announce that they are folding. The last player remaining wins the pot, even if the hand has not reached the river. You can win by having the best hand at showdown or by being the only player who has not folded. Rules reference: PokerStars’ Texas Hold’em rules . Comic 04 · Published October 14, 2026 Two hole cards, one hole card, or none: your best five-card hand decides a Hold’em showdown. A sixth card never breaks a tie. Poker 101: The Best Five Cards Win! Artwork generated with Google Gemini. Open the full image or save the comic . Original Gemini share .

At showdown, choose your strongest five-card combination from your two hole cards and the five community cards. Hold’em allows zero, one or two hole cards. Equal best five-card hands split the pot; neither a sixth card nor a suit breaks the tie. The small AI-drawn card faces can be inconsistent. The complete deals below are separate, illustrative examples of the comic’s lessons. Playing the board does not guarantee a split: an opponent may improve on it.

The showdown A player expects an ace in their hand to settle the result. The dealer slows them down: first identify the best five cards available to each player still in the hand. How it works Your private cards do not have to appear in your final hand. Select whichever five-card combination is strongest, whether it uses both hole cards, just one, or the entire board. Example 1: two hole cards You hold A♥ K♥. The board is A♣ K♠ 9♣ 5♦ 2♠. Your best hand is A♥ A♣ K♥ K♠ 9♣: two pair, aces and kings, with a nine kicker. Both hole cards contribute. Example 2: one hole card You hold J♠ 3♣. The board is A♣ K♦ Q♥ 10♠ 2♦. Your best hand is A♣ K♦ Q♥ J♠ 10♠: an ace-high straight. Only your jack contributes; the three is outside your best five. Example 3: zero hole cards You hold 2♦ 3♣. The board is 8♣ 7♦ 6♥ 5♠ 4♣. Your best hand is the board’s eight-high straight. Neither hole card improves it. An opponent holding a nine could make a nine-high straight and beat you. The tiebreaker myth On that same 8♣ 7♦ 6♥ 5♠ 4♣ board, A♥ K♥ and Q♠ J♦ both play the eight-high straight. The ace does not help because it is outside the best five. If these are the only two players contesting the pot, they split it.

A kicker matters when it belongs to the best five-card hand. With a pair, compare the pair first, then the three side cards in order. With a straight, all five places are already occupied: compare the highest card in each straight. There is no extra kicker. Try more examples in Which hand wins? and Reading the board . Rules reference: PokerStars’ Texas Hold’em rules . Published by Nolan Kido. Artwork generated with Google Gemini; explanatory text prepared with AI assistance. The written deals are illustrative examples, not recorded hands.
